source.title: Benefit and Cost of Random-Token Replacement under Repeated Data: A Known-Entropy Decomposition and Evidence from Ten Real Corpora

record.tranche_reason: The study reports validation-loss trajectories over training time. They show a fall to a minimum followed by a rise, but no later fall within the reported 32-epoch Korean-web sweep; this refines and challenges the full fall-rise-fall epoch-wise claim in the tested setting.
record.gate_note: Rows record the study's own measurements of validation loss rising after its minimum, including the 32-epoch sweep and reported final-minus-minimum loss terms. The paper also cites prior work on repeated data and non-monotonic loss; those cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study tracks held-out validation loss over training epochs, the measure V2 names, in data-constrained LM pretraining. Its 32-epoch Korean-web sweep (App. C.6, Fig. 6) and Fig. 3 curves show a fall to a minimum within about 5 epochs, then a steep rise with no reported second fall. The study does not set out to test double descent and cites Nakkiran et al. only in passing. So this is a new-setting result (T3), not a targeted refutation (T5).
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Replacement's benefit is a smaller loss rise after the minimum, and its bias cost is present from the start, so stopping point decides size and sign. It helps every non-program-generated corpus tested and harms only the highly redundant census JSON corpus. On the Markov source, the sign turns from harm to help as predictability falls.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains with random-token replacement and measures validation loss under repeated data; it does not reproduce a model-size or sample-size double-descent sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported loss-rise and replacement effects vary with source predictability, corpus, training point, corruption rate, learning-rate schedule, and model scale.

fits_no_version.finding: Random-token replacement shrinks the post-minimum validation-loss rise under repeated data, by about 35-60%, but does not eliminate it. LR decay shrinks the rise only 7-12%, and stronger weight decay leaves much of it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Input-corruption regularization reduces, but does not remove, the overfitting rise in validation loss under multi-epoch repeated-data LM pretraining.

record.problems: The 32-epoch trajectory is reported for one seed. The study measures held-out validation loss, not test error, and does not report a later descent in its epoch sweeps. It tests only two model scales and does not sweep model size or sample count around an interpolation threshold.

untested.parts: No model-size sweep. Only two scales (134M, 336M) are compared, for the augmentation effect.
Training beyond 32 epochs on real corpora is not reported. No label noise is added. No placement relative to an interpolation threshold. Error/accuracy is not measured, only cross-entropy loss.
No capacity sweeps across model classes.
No effective-complexity measure is used to predict peak locations.
No label-noise manipulation and no multiple peaks. Regularization (weight decay, replacement, LR decay) is applied to a monotone post-minimum rise, not a double-descent peak.

missing.what: Validation-loss trajectories for all real corpora over the 22-epoch budget (one seed) and for the Markov source over about 65 epochs. The text describes these as falling to a minimum and then rising, with no second descent.
Abundant-data Markov runs (140M tokens) rise by at most 0.004 nats after their minimum, so the rise appears only with repetition.
Epoch at which validation loss reaches its minimum, across ten corpora, NONE vs REPLACE (2.1–9.3 epochs).

record.verdict_notes: The study measures cross-entropy validation loss, not test error. Absence of a second descent within 32 epochs does not rule out a later one. The setting also lacks the label noise and interpolation-threshold sizing under which Nakkiran et al. report epoch-wise double descent, so limits_scope is used rather than challenges. App. C.4 notes brief rise-then-fall fluctuations near the minimum, affecting early stopping. These are small (at most 0.65 nats at patience 1) and are not described as double descent.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep of test error or interpolation threshold; the 134M and 336M models compare the replacement intervention, not a size-wise double-descent curve.
The study reports an initial fall and subsequent rise in validation loss, but no second fall within its reported trajectories. It does not establish behavior beyond the reported training periods.
No sweep over the number of training samples near an interpolation threshold.
No capacity sweeps across model classes or measurement of risk past an interpolation point.
The loss decomposition does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.

The study examines input-token replacement and weight decay, but does not test label-noise-driven double-descent peaks, multiple peaks, or disappearance of such peaks under optimally tuned regularization.
No re-counting of complexity by effective parameters or test of whether that turns a second-descent curve into an ordinary U-shape.

relationships.condition: Decoder-only LMs (134M, 336M) trained from scratch on repeated 7.4M-token Korean web text, up to 32 epochs, constant LR, one seed
relationships.reason: r1-r4 (Table 19, Fig. 6): the curve falls to a minimum near 5-8 epochs, then rises 1.6-2.8 nats by epoch 32. No second descent appears within the window, with or without replacement.
relationships.display_finding: Loss reached a minimum near epochs 5–8, then rose 1.6–2.8 nats by epoch 32 without a second descent, with or without random-token replacement.

labels.condition: Decoder-only LMs (134M, 336M) trained from scratch on repeated 7.4M-token Korean web text, up to 32 epochs, constant LR, one seed
labels.reason: Rows r1–r4 and Appendix C.6 report an initial decline followed by substantial loss increases, with no second descent reported within 32 epochs. This is an incomplete trajectory in the tested window; later recovery remains untested.

relation.reason: Its held-out validation-loss trajectories over training epochs directly bear on V2's fall-rise-fall claim.

tranche.reason: The repeated-data language-model epoch sweep supplies a result on V2 in a new setting; the study investigates replacement and overfitting rather than reproducing or directly refuting the original double-descent experiment.

source_check.notes: The authors-conclusion paraphrase matches the text. The 32-epoch sweep uses one seed; Table 2 uses three-seed means over the approximately 22-epoch main budget. Interpolation timing and recovery beyond 32 epochs are not established.
